strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in dLLM evaluation—while parallel decoding is promised as a key advantage, standard benchmarks don't expose quality degradation
Strong information-theoretic foundation using conditional total correlation to characterize parallel decoding difficulty; Theorems 1-2 provide principled lower bounds
Excellent synthetic analysis with analytically tractable list operations (Copy, Replace Random, Shuffle) and closed-form accuracy predictions that are empirically validated
Thoughtfully designed benchmark with 17 tasks spanning realistic difficulty levels grounded in C(Y|X); clever use of structurally similar tasks with different dependencies (Sudoku vs Latin Square)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dLLMs, autoregressive baselines, unmasking strategies, and extensive ablations with well-organized supplementary materials
Oracle analysis revealing substantial room for improvement and clear demonstration that adaptive methods (threshold) outperform static approaches (top-k)
Clear, well-written presentation with effective motivation and intuitive examples; findings are clearly stated and supported
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 1 straightforwardly applies Huang et al. (2022)'s result to T-step case; conditional independence issues already identified in Wu et al. (2025) and Feng et al. (2025). Proofs use standard techniques without introducing fundamentally new insights

Benchmark scope limitations: Tasks restricted to short sequences (n≤6 for Waiting Line, 32-64 output tokens maximum)—generalization to practical longer sequences remains unclear. Tasks focused on list operations and ordering; unclear if findings extend to other domains where parallel decoding might excel

Capacity vs. parallelism confound: For small Waiting Line tasks, unclear whether failures stem from parallel decoding or model capacity on novel tasks. Reverse performance varies significantly across models despite C(Y|X)=0 (Fig. 3b), deserving deeper investigation

No wall-clock speed measurements: Despite 'speed-quality tradeoff' being central to motivation, paper reports only theoretical parallelism levels, not actual inference latencies—critical for practical utility claims

Limited solutions: Excellent problem identification but exploration of improvements is sparse. Fine-tuning, CoT, remasking, and uniform diffusion all show limited effectiveness. Paper ends with 'need for innovative methods' without concrete proposals

Fine-tuning setup uses 20K examples per task—unclear if this fairly represents pretrained model behavior. Oracle analysis, while interesting, speculates about per-sample optimization feasibility in practice

Missing critical analyses: No investigation of model size/architecture effects on parallel decoding robustness, limited explanation for why Mercury (commercial) differs from open models, no systematic study of real token dependency distributions across datasets

strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying gap in existing benchmarks for parallel decoding evaluation
Solid information-theoretic analysis with correct Theorems 1-2 connecting conditional total correlation to parallel decoding difficulty
Clever synthetic case studies (list operations) providing analytically tractable analysis and quantitative insights
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dLLMs and unmasking strategies with thorough appendices
Clear problem presentation and generally well-written paper with effective visualizations
weaknesses: Limited novelty: problem already identified in concurrent work (Wu et al. 2025, Feng et al. 2025); theoretical analysis is straightforward application of known information-theoretic concepts
Significant benchmark limitations: extremely small scale (Waiting Line n=3-6), short sequences (32-64 tokens), somewhat synthetic tasks undermine real-world applicability
Insufficient solution exploration: Section 7 shows existing techniques fail but paper offers no concrete improved methods, leaving practitioners with little actionable guidance
Weak theory-practice connection: analysis requires intractable C(Y|X); validation that bounds inform realistic task performance is thin
Incomplete experimental analysis: no statistical significance testing, unexplained anomalies (Mercury underperformance), underdeveloped findings (semi-AR effects in Fig. 5)
Missing critical comparisons: does not deeply engage how this benchmark differs from/improves upon concurrent related work by Wu, Feng, Gong, Ye 2025
Reproducibility concerns: dataset generation details sparse, grammar scoring implementation unclear, no timeline for code/data release
No quantification of practical impact: paper lacks wall-clock speedup-quality analysis or guidance for practitioners choosing between decoding strategies

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Paper identifies important gap in dLLM evaluation that existing benchmarks (GSM8K, HumanEval) don't adequately address
Rigorous theoretical contributions: Theorems 1-2 provide novel formal lower bounds on KL divergence for T-step parallel decoding grounded in conditional total correlation
Elegant synthetic case studies: List operations analysis is mathematically rigorous with precise C(Y|X) calculations validated by empirical results
Comprehensive benchmark design: 17 carefully chosen tasks with clear theoretical grounding, grammar scores capturing token dependencies, and 2D characterization of task properties
Extensive experimental evaluation: Multiple dLLMs tested across numerous unmasking strategies with thorough ablations (fine-tuning, CoT, remasking, KV caching)
Oracle performance analysis: Reveals substantial room for improvement and demonstrates per-sample adaptation could yield significant gains
Excellent presentation: Clear writing, effective figures, logical progression from theory to synthetic to realistic tasks, strong reproducibility
Actionable insights: Key findings clearly demonstrate inadequacy of static methods and limitations of current adaptive approaches
Timely and relevant: Addresses active problem in rapidly developing dLLM field with high practical importance
weaknesses: Lacks concrete solutions: Paper rigorously identifies problems but proposes no new decoding methods; leaves solutions entirely to future work despite oracle analysis suggesting clear paths
Limited sequence length analysis: Main experiments use short sequences (≤32-64 tokens); unclear if findings scale to realistic long-form generation (>100 tokens)
Missing computational analysis: No actual latency or speedup measurements provided; speed-quality tradeoff expressed theoretically but not in practical wall-clock terms
Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; only 100 samples per task makes it unclear if differences between methods are significant
Simplistic evaluation metrics: Grammar metric uses basic language-tool-python; perplexity or human evaluation would strengthen Text Writing results
Incomplete semi-autoregressive analysis: Figure 5 shows conflicting task preferences yet no adaptive block-size strategy explored despite clear indication needed
Underexplored Mercury results: Interesting reversed trends (opposite of open-source models) noted but lack deep investigation into underlying causes
Theory-practice gap: Theoretical analysis assumes ideal models learn perfectly when C(Y|X)=0, but Replace Index fine-tuning shows this assumption doesn't always hold
Limited comparison scope: No comparison with orthogonal speedup approaches (speculative decoding variants, pruning methods, etc.)
Some task design choices questionable: Words-to-Sentence somewhat artificial; limited coverage of domains where dLLMs might naturally excel

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real gap in dLLM evaluation: While parallel decoding limitations from conditional independence are known, adequate characterization and benchmarking are lacking

Solid theoretical framework: Theorems 1-2 establish sound lower bounds on parallel decoding error in terms of conditional total correlation, with proofs that are mathematically correct and validated empirically

Carefully designed benchmark spanning diverse difficulty levels: PARALLELBENCH intelligently ranges from C(Y|X)=0 tasks (Copy, Replace Index) to C(Y|X)→∞ (Shuffle), with grammar-based evaluation better capturing token-level dependencies than standard metrics

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: Multiple dLLMs tested, diverse unmasking strategies compared, extensive ablations (fine-tuning, CoT, remasking samplers), results consistent across models and methods

Clear and actionable empirical insights: Task-dependent performance patterns align with theory; oracle analysis quantifies room for improvement; Mercury results validate core thesis; fine-tuning results confirm theoretical predictions
High-quality presentation: Effective motivation, well-structured narrative, excellent figures (particularly Figures 1 and 6), thorough appendix
Practical benchmark contribution: PARALLELBENCH demonstrates effectiveness across dLLMs and autoregressive models, will be valuable for community developing efficient inference methods
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Core insights about conditional independence causing degradation are known; Theorem 1 applies prior results (Huang et al., 2022) mechanically; T-step extension and Theorem 2 monotonicity are natural but incremental contributions

Artificial evaluation scope potentially limiting generalizability: Short output sequences (32-64 tokens) intentionally chosen to isolate effects but create unrealistic setting; Section D.5 shows longer sequences (n=21-24) exhibit different patterns where model capacity dominates

Primarily diagnostic without algorithmic contributions: Excels at identifying problems but Section 7 shows existing techniques provide minimal improvements; oracle gap (~30%) revealed but no concrete methods proposed to close it; missing research directions for solutions

Benchmark tasks may not reflect realistic language model usage: List operations are somewhat artificial; grammar scoring is rule-based and limited; puzzles are niche cases; tasks explicitly designed to expose vulnerabilities rather than reflect natural difficulty

Incomplete separation of model capacity from parallelization effects: Despite using small n, confounds remain (e.g., Reverse task shows high variance despite C(Y|X)=0); dramatic result differences (e.g., Mercury Latin Square 59% vs. autoregressive 98%) unclear whether from models or parallelization

Semi-autoregressive optimization shows task-dependent conflicts without resolution: Figure 5 demonstrates opposite optimal block lengths for different task categories but provides no principled approach to adaptive selection

Reproducibility concerns: Benchmark generation relies on Gemini 2.5 Pro API; some implementation details underspecified (oracle computation, hyperparameter justification); long-term API availability uncertain

Limited exploration of alternative diffusion variants: Focus primarily on masked diffusion; uniform transition matrix (Section E.5) receives superficial treatment; generalization to other parallel decoding paradigms (beyond Medusa in appendix) unclear

strengths: Sound information-theoretic framework using conditional total correlation to quantify parallel decoding difficulty
Analytically tractable synthetic case studies (list operations) with theoretical predictions validated empirically
Comprehensive benchmark with 17 tasks spanning realistic scenarios (Waiting Line, Text Writing, Puzzles)
Extensive empirical evaluation of multiple dLLMs and unmasking strategies with detailed appendix
Clear documentation that parallel decoding causes quality degradation even on simple tasks
Oracle analysis revealing substantial gap between current methods and optimal per-sample adaptation
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core insight that parallel decoding loses token dependencies is well-known from prior work (Wu et al. 2025, Feng et al. 2025); theoretical contributions are incremental extensions of Huang et al. (2022)
Benchmark uses short sequences (n∈{3,4,5,6}) to isolate parallel decoding from capacity effects, but this undermines realism and makes findings less representative of actual use cases
Tasks are somewhat artificial (shuffling customer names) despite 'realistic' framing; Table 7-9 show autoregressive LLMs don't achieve perfect scores, contradicting claims of 'triviality'
No proposed solutions: Section 7 explores fine-tuning, CoT, remasking, etc., but none substantially improve speed-quality tradeoffs, limiting actionability
Theory-practice gap: theorems assume ideal models but empirical validation is limited to fine-tuned LLaDA; unclear how much degradation comes from theoretical limits vs. model imperfection

Incomplete comparison with prior work: GSM8K/HumanEval DO show parallelism degradation (Fig. 26), so arguments for why they're insufficient lack rigor; fairness of comparing parallel dLLMs to one-by-one autoregressive models is questionable

Overstated claims: paper claims tasks are 'trivial for humans and AR-LLMs' but provides mixed evidence; 'first benchmark for dLLMs' overlooks that challenges apply to other parallel generation methods
Limited evaluation: no error bars/significance tests despite LLM stochasticity; more nuanced metrics (semantic similarity, human evaluation) needed beyond exact-match accuracy
Recent unmasking methods (Section E.1) relegated to appendix; reproducibility concerns regarding Gemini-generated task data

strengths: Addresses important and underexplored problem: parallel decoding tradeoffs in dLLMs with clear practical relevance
Rigorous theoretical foundation: Theorems 1-2 provide formal bounds on quality degradation with sound proofs and proper extension to T-step generation

Excellent benchmark design: ParallelBench is well-motivated with 17 carefully designed tasks spanning realistic difficulty levels; tasks are trivial for humans/autoregressive LLMs but challenging for dLLMs
Thorough synthetic analysis: List operations provide analytically tractable case studies with explicit accuracy predictions (e.g., Eq. 5 for Shuffle) confirmed empirically
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple dLLM variants, extensive unmasking strategies tested, extensive ablations, oracle analysis reveals substantial room for improvement
Well-presented: Clear writing, effective visualizations (especially Figures 1, 6), concrete examples, detailed experimental specifications enable reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 1 extends prior work (Huang et al. 2022) relatively straightforwardly; conditional total correlation and subadditivity are established tools; contribution is primarily quantification rather than new concepts

Benchmark limited to short sequences (n=3-6): Section D.5 reveals longer sequences (n=21-24) show model capacity as confounding factor, undermining applicability to practical scenarios; unclear how insights transfer to realistic generation

Lack of solution-oriented contributions: Paper excels at diagnosis but offers limited guidance on solutions; Section 7 shows existing techniques provide minimal improvements; no novel methods proposed to address identified limitations

Evaluation metric concerns: Grammar score (binary 0/1) is crude; Section D.6 reveals BERTScore/ROUGE-L are 'substantially less sensitive to parallelism,' raising questions about whether using most-sensitive-to-degradation metrics risks confirmation bias

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; 100 samples per task is reasonable but variance not discussed; some differences appear marginal without uncertainty quantification

Inconsistent experimental design: Different prompting strategies (one-shot vs zero-shot) across categories, different temperature settings, different metrics complicate interpretation and cross-task comparison
